title: "daily bread"
hook: "daily bread" — just today's; the prayer that refuses to hoard

segments.voice: Yesterday, line two of the Lord's Prayer: thy kingdom come. Not a place far off, a way things could be, here. Your line was here, now, would be fine. Did you make one corner a little better? Now, line three. Day six.

Open your fridge, or your pantry, or the notes app where you keep your plans. Most of us are quietly stocking up. The extra pack of pasta. The backup charger. The savings account we check at 2am. It makes sense. Tomorrow is scary, and a full shelf feels like safety. Now here's the middle of the Lord's Prayer. After the Father and the kingdom, the prayer finally asks for something for us. And what it asks for is small. Not a full shelf. Not the year sorted. Just bread. Just today's. We're on line three of five, and it's the line that refuses to hoard.
screen: `THE SHELF WE KEEP STOCKING.` → `THE PRAYER FINALLY ASKS FOR US.` → `JUST TODAY'S.`

segments.voice: Here's the line, from Matthew: "Give us this day our daily bread." Bread, in that world, meant food, the thing you actually ate to stay alive. So this is the plainest request in the prayer. And it has an old story behind it. In Exodus, the people of Israel are in the desert, hungry, and every morning something to eat lies on the ground. They call it manna. The rule is simple: gather what you need for today. Some people gather extra and keep it overnight, and by morning it has spoiled. The Bible puts the result this way: "he that gathered much had nothing over, and he that gathered little had no lack." Enough for everyone. Nothing to stockpile. Many who first heard Jesus teach this prayer knew that story by heart. Now an honest puzzle. The Greek word translated daily is epiousios, and it almost never appears anywhere else. An early Christian writer, Origen, thought the Gospel writers may have coined it. It might mean for today. It might mean for tomorrow. It might mean what we need to exist. Jerome, translating the Bible into Latin, used two different words for it in two different Gospels. Nobody knows for sure. Churches hear it in different ways, too. Catholic and Orthodox Christians often hear in daily bread both ordinary food and the bread of communion. Many Protestants hear first the plain food on the table, and some add the word of God. Almost everyone agrees on the last thing: the word is us. Give us. Not give me. Enough for today, for everyone at the table.
screen: `BREAD — THE PLAINEST REQUEST.` · `MANNA: GATHER ONLY TODAY'S.` · `EPIOUSIOS — NOBODY IS SURE.` · then, large: `GIVE US, NOT GIVE ME.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, think of what you'll eat today. Just today. On the second, notice one thing you're worried won't be enough tomorrow, and set it down for one breath. On the third, if you pray, you can say the line: give us this day our daily bread. If you don't, simply notice: for today, there is enough.
Line three of the Lord's Prayer. Give us this day our daily bread: a small request, for today, for all of us. Sixth word.
Your line to carry: enough for today. Before you buy one more thing today, pause and ask: is there enough already? And if there's extra, share it. Day six.

howItsDone: Christians pray "give us this day our daily bread" each time they say the Lord's Prayer, and many say a short grace before meals. Catholic and Orthodox Christians often connect the line with the bread of communion as well as ordinary food.

original.note: Greek: the word behind "daily." it almost never appears outside the Lord's Prayer, and its exact meaning is still debated.

trapdoor: what you thought: daily bread just means food.
what it means: enough for today, for all of us, like manna in the desert. the prayer that refuses to hoard.
what a scholar hears: epiousios is almost unknown outside this prayer. Jerome's Latin used supersubstantialem in Matthew and cotidianum in Luke, and the debate has never closed.

notes: Origen (On Prayer 27) suggests epiousios was coined by the evangelists; stated as 'thought the Gospel writers may have coined it'. Confirm.
Vulgate: Matthew 6:11 'supersubstantialem', Luke 11:3 'cotidianum' (in the trapdoor). Confirm spellings.
Church readings of daily bread (Catholic and Orthodox: food and the Eucharist; many Protestants: plain food first, some add the word of God) stated broadly; confirm fair to each.
Manna story compresses Exodus 16:16–21 (gather an omer each; kept overnight bred worms and stank; the Sabbath exception is left out). Confirm the simplification is acceptable.
